04 · Decision brief

What school leaders should act on

Each recommendation begins with a measured signal and ends with a practical next step.

01 · CAPACITY992

Protect the high-capacity core.

Lamont and Widener contain 47% of all 2,098 listed seats. Disruptions in these two libraries would affect system capacity disproportionately.

02 · STUDY MODE45 / 58

Make noise expectations visible.

Only 45 records are Silent or Whispers, while 58 are Chatter. Consistent online and in-building noise labels would reduce mismatch.

03 · COLLABORATION32 / 27

Audit rooms before buying equipment.

Only 32 spaces list displays and 27 list whiteboards. First verify which reservable rooms truly lack them, then target upgrades.

Recommended implementation plan

Move from directory to service evidence.

  1. Standardize and verify.Require the same fields for every record—capacity, noise, access, power, reservation, and equipment—and label unknown values explicitly.Measure: 95% field completion
  2. Pilot anonymous demand counts.Count occupied seats in Lamont and Widener during broad morning, afternoon, evening, and late-night blocks for four representative weeks.Measure: utilization by time block
  3. Validate student priorities.Run a short anonymous survey that asks students to rank features and rate broad space types, without names, contact details, or device tracking.Measure: ≥200 responses across schools

06 · Data & methods

A documented, reproducible snapshot

Collected 21 September 2026 from Harvard Library’s public APIs. No names, contact details, personal locations, medical information, or behavioral histories were collected.

QUESTION

What space best fits the work?

The unit is one named room or study area. The users are students choosing a setting and library teams prioritizing facility information and services.

COVERAGE

103 records, not a hand-picked sample

The project downloaded every room returned by the public space-finder API, then joined 13 represented libraries and expanded 19 amenities into binary fields.

SCORING

Eight signals, visibly weighted

Published fields become 0–100 signals for quiet, privacy, collaboration, technology, reservation, comfort, access, and capacity. The fit score is their normalized weighted average.

CODING RULE

“Not listed” is not “absent”

A binary 1 means an amenity is explicitly listed. A 0 means it was not listed in that record. This protects the analysis from claiming more than the source supports.

Key units and definitions

FieldUnitDefinition
SeatscountPublished designed capacity; one record has no value.
NoisecategoryOfficial codes: 0 Silent, 1 Whispers, 2 Chatter.
Coordinatesdecimal degreesPublished latitude and longitude for the room or parent library.
Amenities0 / 1Nineteen published indicators including accessibility, charging, display, food, private desks, tech, and whiteboards.
Fit score0–100 model pointsNormalized weighted average of eight signals; not a satisfaction rating.
Read the complete one-page methodology →

Limitations and uncertainty

  • Directory boundary: classrooms, residences, cafés, outdoor areas, and any spaces missing from the API are outside scope.
  • Documentation bias: richer records can score better even when another room has the same unlisted amenity.
  • No demand data: capacity is not occupancy; the project cannot identify crowding or wait times.
  • No satisfaction data: the score models fit and cannot prove student preference or wellbeing.
  • Access varies: hours, eligibility, booking rules, and equipment change; users must check the live source.
  • Weights are judgments: presets are transparent analytic choices, not Harvard policy.
